questions.text: Which mineral element is needed by green plants for the formation of chlorophyll?
questions.explanation:
Concept: Magnesium is the central atom of the chlorophyll molecule. Without it leaves turn yellow (chlorosis).
Step 1: Recall the structure of a chlorophyll molecule.
Step 2: Its centre holds one atom of a metal.
Step 3: That metal is magnesium, so a plant short of magnesium has pale yellow leaves.
Answer: Magnesium.
Common mistake: Calcium builds cell walls, potassium helps enzymes and water balance, and sodium is not needed by most plants.
Similar example: A plant lacks nitrogen. What is the leaf symptom? Yellowing of the leaves (chlorosis).
Tip: Magnesium goes into Chlorophyll, Mg for Make green.

questions.text: The enzyme in saliva that converts starch to maltose is
questions.explanation:
Concept: Salivary amylase (ptyalin) begins starch digestion in the mouth. Pepsin acts on protein in the stomach, lipase on fats and trypsin on protein in the small intestine.
Step 1: Saliva is released in the mouth, where digestion of starch begins.
Step 2: Match the enzyme to the substrate: starch is broken down by an amylase.
Step 3: The amylase in saliva is salivary amylase (ptyalin).
Answer: Salivary amylase.
Common mistake: Pepsin digests protein, lipase digests fat and trypsin digests protein in the small intestine.
Similar example: Which enzyme digests starch in the small intestine? Pancreatic amylase.

questions.text: The dental formula of an adult human is
questions.explanation:
Concept: Each half of each jaw has 2 incisors, 1 canine, 2 premolars and 3 molars: (2+1+2+3) x 2 x 2 = 32 teeth.
Step 1: Write the teeth for ONE half of each jaw: 2 incisors, 1 canine, 2 premolars, 3 molars.
Step 2: Add them up: 2 + 1 + 2 + 3 = 8 teeth per half jaw.
Step 3: Multiply by 4 half jaws: 8 x 4 = 32 teeth, which matches an adult human.
Answer: I 2/2, C 1/1, PM 2/2, M 3/3.
Common mistake: The other formulas have the wrong number of premolars or molars, so the total is not 32.
Similar example: How many teeth does a child have? 20 milk teeth: I 2/2, C 1/1, M 2/2.
Tip: Remember 2-1-2-3.

questions.text: The blood vessel that carries oxygenated blood from the lungs to the heart is the
questions.explanation:
Concept: The pulmonary vein is an exception: a vein carrying oxygenated blood. It enters the left atrium.
Step 1: Blood from the lungs has just picked up oxygen, so it is oxygenated.
Step 2: It travels back to the left atrium of the heart.
Step 3: The vessel doing this is the pulmonary vein.
Answer: Pulmonary vein.
Common mistake: The pulmonary artery carries blood to the lungs. The aorta and vena cava serve the whole body.
Similar example: Which vessel brings deoxygenated blood from the body to the right atrium? Vena cava.
Tip: Pulmonary vein is the one vein that carries oxygenated blood.

questions.text: Which blood component is mainly responsible for blood clotting?
questions.explanation:
Concept: Platelets (thrombocytes) release substances that start the clotting process, forming a fibrin mesh over the wound.
Step 1: When a vessel is cut, something must plug the hole and start the clot.
Step 2: That is done by the tiny cell fragments called platelets.
Step 3: They release substances that change fibrinogen to fibrin threads.
Answer: Platelets.
Common mistake: Red cells carry oxygen. Lymphocytes and monocytes are white cells that fight infection.
Similar example: Which cells carry oxygen? Red blood cells.

questions.text: Water enters the root hair cells of a plant mainly by
questions.explanation:
Concept: Soil water has a higher water potential than the cell sap, so water moves into the root hair across the partially permeable membrane by osmosis.
Step 1: Soil water is dilute, so it has a higher water potential than the cell sap.
Step 2: Water moves from high to low water potential across the partially permeable membrane.
Step 3: That movement of water is osmosis.
Answer: Osmosis.
Common mistake: Guttation is loss of water from leaf margins. Translocation moves food. Phagocytosis is taking in solid particles.
Similar example: How do mineral salts enter root hairs? By active transport.

questions.text: The products of anaerobic respiration in yeast are
questions.explanation:
Concept: Yeast ferments glucose without oxygen: glucose gives ethanol + carbon dioxide + a little energy.
Step 1: Yeast respires without oxygen, so it ferments glucose.
Step 2: Write the equation: glucose gives ethanol and carbon dioxide, with a little energy.
Step 3: This is why dough rises and why brewing makes alcohol.
Answer: Ethanol and carbon dioxide.
Common mistake: Lactic acid is made in muscle. Water and carbon dioxide come from aerobic respiration.
Similar example: What does a muscle make when it is short of oxygen? Lactic acid.
Tip: Muscle makes lactic acid. Yeast makes ethanol.

questions.text: The main organ of gaseous exchange in a fish is the
questions.explanation:
Concept: Water passes over the gill filaments, where oxygen diffuses into the blood and carbon dioxide diffuses out.
Step 1: Fish live in water, which has dissolved oxygen.
Step 2: Water flows over thin gill filaments full of blood vessels.
Step 3: Oxygen diffuses in and carbon dioxide diffuses out.
Answer: Gill.
Common mistake: Fish have no lungs. The swim bladder keeps them buoyant and the skin plays only a small part.
Similar example: Which organ do tadpoles use? Gills.

questions.text: The structural and functional unit of the kidney is the
questions.explanation:
Concept: Each kidney contains about a million nephrons. Each one filters blood and forms urine.
Step 1: The kidney filters blood and forms urine.
Step 2: Each kidney contains about one million small filtering tubes.
Step 3: Each tube with its blood capillaries is a nephron.
Answer: Nephron.
Common mistake: A neurone is the unit of the nervous system, an alveolus of the lung and a villus of the small intestine.
Similar example: What is the unit of the nervous system? The neurone.

questions.text: The organ that converts excess amino acids to urea is the
questions.explanation:
Concept: In deamination the liver removes the amino group from excess amino acids and converts it to urea. The kidney then excretes the urea.
Step 1: The body cannot store amino acids.
Step 2: The liver removes the amino group from the excess in a process called deamination.
Step 3: The nitrogen part is turned into urea, which the kidney removes.
Answer: Liver.
Common mistake: The kidney only removes urea. The pancreas and spleen do not make urea.
Similar example: Where is bile made? In the liver.

questions.text: A joint that allows movement in all directions is the
questions.explanation:
Concept: In a ball-and-socket joint, as at the shoulder and hip, the rounded head of one bone fits into a cup in the other, giving the widest movement.
Step 1: Compare how each joint moves.
Step 2: A hinge moves in one direction only and a gliding joint slides a little.
Step 3: A ball-and-socket joint (shoulder, hip) swings in every direction.
Answer: Ball-and-socket joint.
Common mistake: A hinge joint (elbow, knee) bends in one plane. A pivot joint only rotates. A gliding joint only slides.
Similar example: Which joint lets the head turn from side to side? Pivot joint.

questions.text: The biceps and triceps muscles are described as antagonistic because
options: When one contracts the other relaxes
They are attached to the same bone
questions.explanation:
Concept: Muscles can only pull. A pair working in opposite directions is needed to bend and straighten a limb.
Step 1: A muscle can only pull, never push.
Step 2: So one muscle bends the limb and another must straighten it.
Step 3: When one contracts the other relaxes, so they work in opposite ways.
Answer: When one contracts the other relaxes.
Common mistake: They do not contract together. They are attached to different bones and are both voluntary.
Similar example: When the biceps contracts the forearm does what? It bends upward.

questions.text: The transfer of pollen grains from the anther to the stigma of the same flower is
questions.explanation:
Concept: Self-pollination happens within one flower or between flowers of the same plant. Cross-pollination needs a different plant of the same species.
Step 1: Find where the pollen starts and ends: anther to stigma.
Step 2: Check if the same flower or plant is involved: yes, the same flower.
Step 3: That is self-pollination.
Answer: Self-pollination.
Common mistake: Cross-pollination needs a different plant. Fertilisation is the fusion of gametes after pollination.
Similar example: Pollen carried to another plant of the same species by wind is cross-pollination.

questions.text: The part of a flower that develops into a fruit after fertilisation is the
questions.explanation:
Concept: After fertilisation the ovary wall becomes the fruit and the ovules become seeds.
Step 1: After fertilisation the flower changes.
Step 2: The ovules become the seeds.
Step 3: The ovary wall becomes the fruit.
Answer: Ovary.
Common mistake: The ovule becomes the seed, not the fruit. The style and petals wither.
Similar example: Which part of the flower becomes the seed? Ovule.

questions.text: The hormone that triggers ovulation in the menstrual cycle is
questions.explanation:
Concept: A surge of LH from the pituitary gland near the middle of the cycle causes the mature follicle to release the egg.
Step 1: Ovulation is the release of the egg from the ovary.
Step 2: It takes place near day 14 of the menstrual cycle.
Step 3: A sudden surge of LH from the pituitary gland triggers it.
Answer: Luteinising hormone (LH).
Common mistake: FSH starts the follicle growing. Oestrogen thickens the uterus lining. Progesterone keeps it thick.
Similar example: Which hormone makes the follicle grow? FSH.

questions.text: Yeast reproduces asexually mainly by
questions.explanation:
Concept: A small outgrowth, the bud, forms on the parent cell, receives a nucleus and breaks away.
Step 1: Look at a yeast cell under the microscope.
Step 2: A small outgrowth forms on the side of the parent.
Step 3: The nucleus divides, one nucleus enters the outgrowth and it breaks off. This is budding.
Answer: Budding.
Common mistake: Amoeba and bacteria divide by binary fission. Sporangia are found in Mucor and ferns.
Similar example: How does Hydra reproduce asexually? By budding as well.

questions.text: Which plant hormone promotes cell elongation in stems?
questions.explanation:
Concept: Auxins (indole acetic acid) are made in shoot tips and make cells on the shaded side elongate, which is why shoots grow towards light.
Step 1: Plant stems bend towards light.
Step 2: The cause is a hormone made in the shoot tip that makes cells longer on the shaded side.
Step 3: This hormone is auxin.
Answer: Auxin.
Common mistake: Ethylene ripens fruit, abscisic acid closes stomata and cytokinin promotes cell division.
Similar example: Which hormone breaks the dormancy of seeds? Gibberellin.

questions.text: The part of the brain that controls balance and posture is the
questions.explanation:
Concept: The cerebellum coordinates muscular movement, posture and balance.
Step 1: Balance needs constant adjustment of the muscles.
Step 2: That coordination is the work of the cerebellum, at the back of the brain.
Step 3: The cerebrum handles thinking and the medulla controls breathing.
Answer: Cerebellum.
Common mistake: The cerebrum is for thought and memory. The medulla controls heartbeat and breathing. The hypothalamus controls temperature.
Similar example: Which part controls heartbeat? Medulla oblongata.

questions.text: Insulin is secreted by the
options: Islets of Langerhans in the pancreas
questions.explanation:
Concept: Beta cells in the islets of Langerhans release insulin when blood sugar is high. It lowers blood sugar.
Step 1: Insulin lowers the level of blood glucose.
Step 2: It is made by beta cells in a part of an organ that also makes digestive juices.
Step 3: That organ is the pancreas, and the cells are the islets of Langerhans.
Answer: Islets of Langerhans in the pancreas.
Common mistake: The liver stores glycogen, the adrenal glands make adrenaline and the thyroid makes thyroxine.
Similar example: Which hormone raises blood sugar? Glucagon.

questions.text: The part of the eye that controls the amount of light entering it is the
questions.explanation:
Concept: The iris has circular and radial muscles that change the size of the pupil: it gets smaller in bright light and larger in dim light.
Step 1: Light must be regulated so the retina is not damaged.
Step 2: The coloured ring of muscle changes the size of the pupil.
Step 3: That ring is the iris.
Answer: Iris.
Common mistake: The cornea refracts light, the retina detects it and the lens focuses it.
Similar example: Which part of the eye detects light? The retina.

questions.text: The association between Rhizobium bacteria and the roots of leguminous plants is an example of
questions.explanation:
Concept: Rhizobium fixes nitrogen for the plant, and the plant gives the bacteria food and shelter. Both benefit.
Step 1: The bacteria live in nodules on the roots of beans and groundnut.
Step 2: They fix nitrogen for the plant, and the plant gives them sugars and shelter.
Step 3: Both gain, so this is mutualism.
Answer: Mutualism.
Common mistake: In parasitism one gains and the other is harmed. In commensalism one gains and the other is unaffected.
Similar example: Lichen is an alga and a fungus. What is this relationship? Mutualism.

questions.text: In the food chain grass, grasshopper, toad, snake, the toad is a
questions.explanation:
Concept: Grass is the producer, the grasshopper is the primary consumer, the toad eats the grasshopper so it is the secondary consumer, and the snake is the tertiary consumer.
Step 1: Number the levels: grass (producer), grasshopper, toad, snake.
Step 2: The grasshopper eats the producer, so it is the primary consumer.
Step 3: The toad eats the grasshopper, so the toad is the secondary consumer.
Answer: Secondary consumer.
Common mistake: Primary consumer is the grasshopper. The snake is the tertiary consumer.
Similar example: In grass, goat, lion, who is the secondary consumer? The lion.

questions.text: Which of the following is an abiotic factor of an ecosystem?
questions.explanation:
Concept: Abiotic factors are the non-living parts of the environment, such as temperature, light, pH, rainfall and humidity.
Step 1: Abiotic means non-living.
Step 2: Predators, parasites and decomposers are all living organisms.
Step 3: Only temperature is a physical factor.
Answer: Temperature.
Common mistake: Predators, parasites and decomposers are biotic factors.
Similar example: Which of these is abiotic: rainfall or termites? Rainfall.

questions.text: Which of the following organisms converts ammonium compounds in the soil into nitrates?
questions.explanation:
Concept: Nitrosomonas turns ammonia into nitrite and Nitrobacter turns nitrite into nitrate. These are the nitrifying bacteria.
Step 1: Ammonium compounds come from decay of proteins and urea.
Step 2: Bacteria turn them into nitrites and then nitrates, a process called nitrification.
Step 3: These are the nitrifying bacteria.
Answer: Nitrifying bacteria.
Common mistake: Denitrifying bacteria return nitrogen to the air. Rhizobium and blue-green algae fix nitrogen gas.
Similar example: Which bacteria turn nitrate to nitrogen gas? Denitrifying bacteria.

questions.text: A soil that is rich in humus, drains well and also holds water is
questions.explanation:
Concept: Loam is a mixture of sand, silt and clay with organic matter, which gives good drainage, aeration and water retention. It is the best soil for farming.
Step 1: Look for a soil that drains well and also keeps some water.
Step 2: Sandy soil drains too fast and clay soil is waterlogged.
Step 3: Loam has a mix of sand, silt and clay with humus.
Answer: Loamy soil.
Common mistake: Sandy soil is dry and poor. Clay soil is sticky and badly aerated. Laterite is poor in humus.
Similar example: Which soil is best for farming? Loam.

questions.text: The gas mainly responsible for the greenhouse effect and global warming is
questions.explanation:
Concept: Carbon dioxide traps heat in the atmosphere. It is released by burning fuels and by deforestation.
Step 1: The greenhouse effect is the trapping of heat in the atmosphere.
Step 2: Gases that do this come from burning fuel and from breathing.
Step 3: The most abundant of them is carbon dioxide.
Answer: Carbon dioxide.
Common mistake: Oxygen, nitrogen and argon do not trap much heat.
Similar example: Name another greenhouse gas. Methane.
Tip: Methane and CFCs also add to the greenhouse effect.

questions.text: The biome characterised by tall grasses with scattered trees and a marked dry season is the
questions.explanation:
Concept: Savanna grassland has a long dry season, so the trees are scattered and deciduous, and bush fires are common.
Step 1: Note the clues: tall grasses, scattered trees, a dry season.
Step 2: Rainforest has dense trees all year, tundra is cold and desert has very little rain.
Step 3: The match is savanna.
Answer: Savanna.
Common mistake: Tropical rainforest has thick trees and heavy rain. Tundra is cold. Desert is very dry.
Similar example: Where do bush fires occur often? Savanna.

questions.text: The physical appearance of an organism for a particular trait is its
questions.explanation:
Concept: Phenotype is what can be seen or measured. Genotype is the genetic make-up that produces it.
Step 1: Find what is observed: the appearance.
Step 2: Genetic make-up is the genotype.
Step 3: What can be seen is the phenotype.
Answer: Phenotype.
Common mistake: Genotype is the genes. An allele is one form of a gene. A genome is all the genes.
Similar example: A plant has genotype Tt. What is its phenotype? Tall.
Tip: Phenotype = Physical.

questions.text: When two heterozygous tall plants (Tt x Tt) are crossed, the phenotypic ratio of the offspring is
questions.explanation:
Concept: TT, Tt, Tt are tall and tt is short, giving a 3:1 ratio. The genotype ratio is 1 TT : 2 Tt : 1 tt.
Step 1: Write the cross: Tt x Tt.
Step 2: Gametes: T and t from each parent. Combine them: TT, Tt, Tt, tt.
Step 3: Three plants have at least one T, so they are tall. One is tt, which is short. Ratio 3 : 1.
Answer: 3 tall : 1 short.
Common mistake: 1 : 1 comes from a test cross. 'All tall' would come from TT x tt.
Similar example: Cross Tt x tt. What is the ratio of tall to short? 1 : 1.

questions.text: The molecule that carries the hereditary information in most organisms is
questions.explanation:
Concept: Genes are lengths of DNA arranged along the chromosomes. The order of bases in DNA codes for proteins.
Step 1: Genes are inherited from parents.
Step 2: They are made of a long molecule coiled into chromosomes.
Step 3: That molecule is DNA.
Answer: DNA.
Common mistake: ATP is energy currency. RNA polymerase is an enzyme. Glycogen is stored carbohydrate.
Similar example: Which molecule carries amino acids to the ribosome? Transfer RNA.

questions.text: Down's syndrome in humans results from
options: A recessive gene on the X chromosome
questions.explanation:
Concept: Non-disjunction during meiosis gives the child three copies of chromosome 21 (trisomy 21), so the child has 47 chromosomes.
Step 1: A normal human has 46 chromosomes.
Step 2: In Down's syndrome the child has one extra chromosome 21 (trisomy 21).
Step 3: That makes 47 chromosomes in total.
Answer: An extra chromosome 21.
Common mistake: Lack of chromosome 21 or a missing Y is not Down's syndrome.
Similar example: Turner's syndrome is XO. How many chromosomes? 45.

questions.text: The theory of evolution by use and disuse of organs was proposed by
questions.explanation:
Concept: Lamarck suggested that organs used often become stronger, organs not used shrink, and the changes are passed to offspring. This is now rejected.
Step 1: Recall who explained the long neck of a giraffe by stretching.
Step 2: That person said that organs used often grow and are passed on.
Step 3: This was Lamarck.
Answer: Lamarck.
Common mistake: Darwin and Wallace proposed natural selection. Mendel founded genetics.
Similar example: Who proposed natural selection? Darwin.

questions.text: Which of the following animals belongs to the phylum Annelida?
questions.explanation:
Concept: Annelids are soft-bodied animals with a body divided into many similar segments. The earthworm is the standard example.
Step 1: Annelids are worms whose bodies are made of many similar rings (segments).
Step 2: Check each option: the snail is a mollusc, the millipede an arthropod and the tapeworm a flatworm.
Step 3: Only the earthworm has a ringed, segmented body.
Answer: Earthworm.
Common mistake: The tapeworm is a flatworm with a flat body, the snail has a shell and the millipede has jointed legs.
Similar example: Is a leech an annelid? Yes. It has a segmented body.
Tip: Annelid means 'little ring'.

questions.text: Viruses are described as borderline between living and non-living things because they
options: Show characteristics of life only inside a host cell
questions.explanation:
Concept: Outside a host cell a virus is inert and can even be crystallised. Inside a host cell it reproduces.
Step 1: Outside a host a virus does nothing and can even be crystallised.
Step 2: Inside a living cell it takes over the cell and makes copies of itself.
Step 3: So it shows life only inside a host cell.
Answer: Show characteristics of life only inside a host cell.
Common mistake: Viruses have no chlorophyll, no cell wall and do not respire.
Similar example: Can a virus reproduce on its own? No, only inside a host cell.

questions.text: Ferns belong to the group
questions.explanation:
Concept: Pteridophytes have true roots, stems and leaves with vascular tissue, but they reproduce by spores, not seeds.
Step 1: Ferns have true roots, stems and leaves with vascular tissue.
Step 2: They reproduce by spores and not by seeds.
Step 3: Plants with that combination are the pteridophytes.
Answer: Pteridophyta.
Common mistake: Bryophytes have no vascular tissue. Thallophytes have no true roots, stems or leaves. Gymnosperms bear seeds.
Similar example: Which group has seeds in cones? Gymnosperms.

questions.text: Which of the following is a crustacean?
questions.explanation:
Concept: Crustaceans have two pairs of antennae and a hard exoskeleton. The spider is an arachnid, the millipede a myriapod and the cockroach an insect.
Step 1: Crustaceans have two pairs of antennae and ten or more legs.
Step 2: Sort the options: spider is an arachnid, millipede is a myriapod and cockroach is an insect.
Step 3: The crab is the crustacean.
Answer: Crab.
Common mistake: The spider has no antennae. The millipede has very many legs and one pair of antennae. The cockroach has six legs.
Similar example: Is a prawn a crustacean? Yes.

questions.text: Mammals differ from other vertebrates in having
options: Moist skin and a tadpole stage
questions.explanation:
Concept: Mammary glands that produce milk and hair or fur are the defining features of mammals.
Step 1: List what is special about mammals: they suckle their young and have hair.
Step 2: Check the options: scales, feathers and moist skin belong to other classes.
Step 3: Mammary glands and body hair are unique to mammals.
Answer: Mammary glands and body hair.
Common mistake: Scales and gills are for fish, feathers and a beak for birds, a tadpole stage for amphibians.
Similar example: Which vertebrates have feathers? Birds.

questions.text: The organelle known as the 'suicide bag' of the cell is the
questions.explanation:
Concept: Lysosomes hold digestive enzymes that break down worn-out organelles and, when the cell dies, the whole cell.
Step 1: The cell must be able to destroy damaged parts.
Step 2: Sacs full of digestive enzymes do this job.
Step 3: They are lysosomes, and if they burst the cell digests itself.
Answer: Lysosome.
Common mistake: Ribosomes make proteins, the Golgi apparatus packs substances and the mitochondrion produces energy.
Similar example: Which organelle digests worn-out organelles? Lysosome.

questions.text: Which plant tissue has cell walls thickened with lignin and mainly gives mechanical support?
questions.explanation:
Concept: Sclerenchyma cells are dead at maturity and strong, and they support the mature parts of the plant.
Step 1: Support in plants comes from tough, thickened cells.
Step 2: Parenchyma is thin-walled, epidermis is a covering and meristem is for division.
Step 3: Sclerenchyma has walls thickened with lignin and gives strength.
Answer: Sclerenchyma.
Common mistake: Parenchyma stores food, meristem divides, and the epidermis covers the plant.
Similar example: Which tissue carries water? Xylem.
Tip: Sclerenchyma is strong, which is why it is used for support.

questions.text: During mitosis, the chromosomes line up at the equator of the cell in
questions.explanation:
Concept: In metaphase the spindle fibres attach to the centromeres and the chromosomes line up in the middle. They separate in anaphase.
Step 1: Put the stages in order: prophase, metaphase, anaphase, telophase.
Step 2: In prophase the chromosomes become visible, and in metaphase they line up at the equator.
Step 3: In anaphase they are pulled apart.
Answer: Metaphase.
Common mistake: In prophase they condense. In anaphase they separate. In telophase new nuclei form.
Similar example: In which stage do the chromatids move to the poles? Anaphase.
Tip: PMAT: Prophase, Metaphase, Anaphase, Telophase.

questions.text: A deficiency of vitamin C in the diet causes
questions.explanation:
Concept: Vitamin C is needed to make collagen. Without it the gums bleed and wounds heal slowly.
Step 1: Vitamin C is needed to make collagen, a part of skin and gums.
Step 2: Without it the gums bleed and wounds are slow to heal.
Step 3: This disease is scurvy.
Answer: Scurvy.
Common mistake: Rickets is lack of vitamin D, beriberi of vitamin B1 and night blindness of vitamin A.
Similar example: Which vitamin is lacking in rickets? Vitamin D.
Tip: Citrus fruits prevent scurvy.

questions.text: A balanced diet is one that contains
options: All the food classes in the correct proportions
questions.explanation:
Concept: A balanced diet supplies carbohydrates, proteins, fats, vitamins, mineral salts, water and roughage in the right amounts.
Step 1: List the food classes: carbohydrates, proteins, fats, vitamins, minerals, water and roughage.
Step 2: A balanced diet has all of them.
Step 3: They must also be in the right proportions.
Answer: All the food classes in the correct proportions.
Common mistake: A diet with only some food classes, or one too rich in fat and sugar, is not balanced.
Similar example: Which food class gives most energy per gram? Fats.

questions.text: The mode of nutrition in which an organism lives on another living organism and harms it is
questions.explanation:
Concept: A parasite takes food from its host and damages it. A saprophyte feeds on dead matter.
Step 1: Look for an organism that lives on a living host.
Step 2: It gains and the host is harmed.
Step 3: That is parasitism.
Answer: Parasitism.
Common mistake: A saprophyte feeds on dead matter, holozoic nutrition is feeding by ingestion and in mutualism both benefit.
Similar example: Is mistletoe a parasite? Yes, it feeds on its host tree.

questions.text: The heart chamber that pumps oxygenated blood to the rest of the body is the
questions.explanation:
Concept: The left ventricle has the thickest wall because it pumps blood through the aorta to the whole body.
Step 1: Oxygenated blood comes from the lungs into the left atrium.
Step 2: It passes into the left ventricle.
Step 3: The left ventricle has the thickest wall and pumps blood out through the aorta.
Answer: Left ventricle.
Common mistake: The right ventricle pumps blood only to the lungs. The atria receive blood.
Similar example: Which chamber pumps blood to the lungs? Right ventricle.

questions.text: Which of the following blood vessels has valves along its length?
questions.explanation:
Concept: Blood in veins is at low pressure. Valves stop it from flowing backwards.
Step 1: Valves are needed where blood pressure is low.
Step 2: Arteries and the aorta have high pressure, and capillaries are too narrow.
Step 3: Veins have valves to stop backflow.
Answer: Vein.
Common mistake: Arteries do not need valves because of the high pressure from the heart.
Similar example: Which vessels have the thickest walls? Arteries.

questions.text: The loss of water vapour from the aerial parts of a plant, mainly through the stomata, is
questions.explanation:
Concept: Transpiration pulls water up the xylem and also cools the leaf.
Step 1: Look at where water is lost: through stomata in the leaves.
Step 2: The form lost is water vapour.
Step 3: This loss is transpiration.
Answer: Transpiration.
Common mistake: Guttation is loss of liquid water. Translocation is movement of food. Osmosis is movement of water across a membrane.
Similar example: What is the liquid loss of water from leaf edges called? Guttation.

questions.text: The part of the cell where aerobic respiration mainly takes place is the
questions.explanation:
Concept: The Krebs cycle and the electron transport chain are in the mitochondrion, which gives most of the ATP.
Step 1: Aerobic respiration needs oxygen and releases a lot of ATP.
Step 2: It takes place in the organelle with folded inner membranes (cristae).
Step 3: That is the mitochondrion.
Answer: Mitochondrion.
Common mistake: The nucleus holds DNA, ribosomes make protein, and the Golgi apparatus packs substances.
Similar example: Where does glycolysis take place? In the cytoplasm.

questions.text: The flap that covers the trachea during swallowing is the
questions.explanation:
Concept: The epiglottis closes the glottis so that food goes into the oesophagus and not the windpipe.
Step 1: When we swallow, food must not enter the windpipe.
Step 2: A flap of cartilage closes over the opening.
Step 3: That flap is the epiglottis.
Answer: Epiglottis.
Common mistake: The larynx is the voice box, the glottis is the opening and the uvula hangs at the back of the mouth.
Similar example: What happens if food enters the trachea? We choke.

questions.text: The main nitrogenous excretory product of mammals is
questions.explanation:
Concept: Urea is made in the liver and removed by the kidneys. Birds and reptiles excrete uric acid and fish excrete ammonia.
Step 1: Proteins that are not needed are broken down in the liver.
Step 2: The poisonous ammonia is turned into a less toxic substance.
Step 3: That substance is urea.
Answer: Urea.
Common mistake: Ammonia is excreted by fish. Uric acid is excreted by birds and insects.
Similar example: What do birds excrete? Uric acid.

questions.text: Glucose is reabsorbed back into the blood in the
questions.explanation:
Concept: All the glucose in the filtrate is normally reabsorbed by active transport in the proximal convoluted tubule.
Step 1: The filtrate leaves the Bowman's capsule with glucose in it.
Step 2: The first coiled tube after the capsule reabsorbs all the glucose by active transport.
Step 3: That tube is the proximal convoluted tubule.
Answer: Proximal convoluted tubule.
Common mistake: Bowman's capsule filters. The loop of Henle and the collecting duct are mainly for water.
Similar example: Which part reabsorbs water under the control of ADH? The collecting duct.

questions.text: The vertebrae that carry the ribs are the
questions.explanation:
Concept: Twelve thoracic vertebrae articulate with the twelve pairs of ribs.
Step 1: Divide the backbone: cervical, thoracic, lumbar, sacral and caudal.
Step 2: The ribs form the chest.
Step 3: The twelve thoracic vertebrae carry them.
Answer: Thoracic vertebrae.
Common mistake: Cervical vertebrae are in the neck and lumbar vertebrae are in the lower back.
Similar example: Which vertebra carries the skull? The atlas (cervical).

questions.text: Which of the following connects a muscle to a bone?
questions.explanation:
Concept: Tendons join muscle to bone, and ligaments join bone to bone.
Step 1: Compare the two connectors: tendon and ligament.
Step 2: A tendon joins muscle to bone.
Step 3: A ligament joins bone to bone.
Answer: Tendon.
Common mistake: Ligaments join bone to bone. Cartilage cushions joints. The cornea is part of the eye.
Similar example: What joins two bones at a joint? Ligament.
Tip: Tendon = muscle to bone. Ligament = bone to bone.

questions.text: In humans, fertilisation normally takes place in the
questions.explanation:
Concept: The sperm meet the egg in the upper part of the oviduct. The zygote then moves to the uterus.
Step 1: The egg is released from the ovary and enters the oviduct.
Step 2: Sperm swim up from the vagina through the uterus.
Step 3: They meet the egg in the oviduct (fallopian tube).
Answer: Fallopian tube (oviduct).
Common mistake: The uterus is where the embryo develops and the ovary produces eggs.
Similar example: Where does implantation take place? In the uterus wall.

questions.text: Which of the following is a stem tuber?
questions.explanation:
Concept: Irish potato is an underground swollen stem with buds ('eyes'). Sweet potato and cassava are root tubers and carrot is a tap root.
Step 1: A stem tuber is an underground stem swollen with food.
Step 2: It has buds (eyes) from which new shoots grow.
Step 3: Irish potato fits this description.
Answer: Irish potato.
Common mistake: Sweet potato and cassava are root tubers, and carrot is a tap root.
Similar example: Is yam a stem tuber? Yes, it is also a stem tuber.

questions.text: The structure that supplies food and oxygen to the foetus in the womb is the
questions.explanation:
Concept: The placenta is where the mother's blood and the foetus's blood come close and exchange substances without mixing.
Step 1: The foetus cannot feed or breathe by itself.
Step 2: A disc-shaped organ allows exchange between mother's blood and foetal blood.
Step 3: That is the placenta.
Answer: Placenta.
Common mistake: The amnion holds the amniotic fluid. The cord carries blood. The endometrium is the lining.
Similar example: What fluid protects the foetus? Amniotic fluid.

questions.text: Which of the following seeds is dispersed by an explosive mechanism?
questions.explanation:
Concept: When a cowpea pod dries it splits suddenly and twists, throwing out the seeds. Coconut uses water, Tridax uses wind and Bidens uses hooks on animals.
Step 1: Dispersal means moving the seed away from the parent.
Step 2: Dry pods that split suddenly throw the seeds out.
Step 3: The cowpea pod does this.
Answer: Cowpea.
Common mistake: Coconut floats on water, Tridax has hairs for the wind and Bidens has hooks for animals.
Similar example: How are the fruits of Bidens dispersed? By animals.

questions.text: Which of the following shows hypogeal germination?
questions.explanation:
Concept: In hypogeal germination the cotyledons stay below the soil. In epigeal germination they are raised above it.
Step 1: In hypogeal germination the cotyledons stay below the ground.
Step 2: In epigeal germination the cotyledons are pushed above the ground.
Step 3: Maize is hypogeal. Cowpea, groundnut and castor oil are epigeal.
Answer: Maize.
Common mistake: Cowpea, groundnut and castor oil seeds push their cotyledons above the soil.
Similar example: Name another hypogeal seed. Broad bean.
Tip: Hypo = below.

questions.text: The rod cells of the retina are responsible for
questions.explanation:
Concept: Rods contain rhodopsin, which is sensitive to dim light but cannot detect colour. Cones detect colour in bright light.
Step 1: The retina has rods and cones.
Step 2: Rods contain rhodopsin and are sensitive to weak light.
Step 3: They cannot detect colour.
Answer: Vision in dim light.
Common mistake: Colour vision depends on cones. Focusing is by the lens. Pupil size is controlled by the iris.
Similar example: Which cells detect colour? Cones.

questions.text: The hormone that prepares the body for 'fight or flight' is
questions.explanation:
Concept: Adrenaline from the adrenal medulla increases heart rate and blood sugar and diverts blood to the muscles.
Step 1: In danger the body needs more energy and blood in the muscles.
Step 2: The adrenal glands release a hormone that speeds up the heartbeat.
Step 3: That hormone is adrenaline.
Answer: Adrenaline.
Common mistake: Insulin lowers blood sugar, thyroxine controls metabolism and oestrogen is a female sex hormone.
Similar example: Which gland produces adrenaline? The adrenal gland.

questions.text: In a reflex arc, the neurone that carries impulses from the spinal cord to the effector is the
questions.explanation:
Concept: The pathway is receptor, sensory neurone, relay neurone, motor neurone, effector.
Step 1: The pathway is receptor, sensory neurone, relay neurone, motor neurone, effector.
Step 2: The impulse goes from the spinal cord to the muscle.
Step 3: The neurone that does this is the motor neurone.
Answer: Motor neurone.
Common mistake: A sensory neurone carries impulses to the spinal cord. The relay neurone connects the two inside the cord.
Similar example: Which neurone carries impulses from the skin to the spinal cord? Sensory neurone.

questions.text: The relationship between a lion and a zebra is
questions.explanation:
Concept: The lion (predator) kills and eats the zebra (prey).
Step 1: One animal kills and eats the other.
Step 2: The lion is the predator and the zebra is the prey.
Step 3: This is predation.
Answer: Predation.
Common mistake: In parasitism the host is not usually killed at once. Commensalism and competition do not involve eating.
Similar example: What is the relationship between a hawk and a chicken? Predation.

questions.text: In an ecosystem the greatest amount of energy is found at the
questions.explanation:
Concept: Producers capture the sunlight. Much energy is lost as heat at each step along the chain, so each level has less.
Step 1: Energy enters the ecosystem as sunlight.
Step 2: Producers capture it by photosynthesis.
Step 3: At every step up the chain about 90% is lost as heat, so producers hold the most.
Answer: Producer level.
Common mistake: Each consumer level holds less energy than the one below it.
Similar example: Which trophic level has the least energy? The top consumer.

questions.text: Which process removes carbon dioxide from the atmosphere?
questions.explanation:
Concept: Green plants use carbon dioxide and water to make glucose in sunlight.
Step 1: Look for a process that uses carbon dioxide.
Step 2: Respiration, decay and combustion all release it.
Step 3: Photosynthesis takes it in to make glucose.
Answer: Photosynthesis.
Common mistake: Respiration, decay and combustion add carbon dioxide to the air.
Similar example: Which process uses oxygen and releases carbon dioxide? Respiration.

questions.text: The enrichment of rivers and lakes by nitrates and phosphates from fertilisers, which causes excessive growth of algae, is called
questions.explanation:
Concept: Fertiliser run-off causes an algal bloom. When the algae die, bacteria use up the oxygen in the water and fish die.
Step 1: Fertiliser washes from the fields into the water.
Step 2: Algae grow too fast and form a bloom.
Step 3: When they die, bacteria use up the oxygen and fish die. This is eutrophication.
Answer: Eutrophication.
Common mistake: Bioaccumulation is the build-up of poisons in the food chain. Transpiration and succession are different processes.
Similar example: Which nutrients mainly cause algal bloom? Nitrates and phosphates.

questions.text: All the individuals of one species living in a particular area at the same time make up a
questions.explanation:
Concept: A population is one species in one place. A community is all the populations in that place.
Step 1: Look at the key words: one species, one area.
Step 2: A group of the same species is a population.
Step 3: A community is made of several populations.
Answer: Population.
Common mistake: A community has many species. An ecosystem includes the environment. A biome is a very large region.
Similar example: What is all the living things in an area called? A community.

questions.text: The uppermost layer of the soil, which is rich in humus, is the
questions.explanation:
Concept: The topsoil (A horizon) contains most of the roots, organisms and organic matter.
Step 1: Soil is made in layers called horizons.
Step 2: The top layer has plant roots, living organisms and humus.
Step 3: It is the topsoil.
Answer: Topsoil.
Common mistake: Subsoil and bedrock are below the topsoil and have less humus.
Similar example: Which layer lies directly above bedrock? Parent rock.

questions.text: The vegetation zone characterised by tall trees arranged in layers and heavy rainfall is the
questions.explanation:
Concept: The rainforest has high rainfall throughout the year and many layers (strata) of vegetation.
Step 1: Look for a zone with heavy rainfall almost all year.
Step 2: The vegetation is dense and has layers: emergent trees, canopy and shrubs.
Step 3: This is the tropical rainforest.
Answer: Tropical rainforest.
Common mistake: Savanna has grass and scattered trees. Desert has very little vegetation.
Similar example: Which zone has grass and scattered trees? Savanna.

questions.text: Different forms of the same gene found at the same locus on homologous chromosomes are
questions.explanation:
Concept: A tall allele (T) and a short allele (t) are alternative forms of the height gene.
Step 1: A gene can have different versions.
Step 2: They sit at the same position on homologous chromosomes.
Step 3: These versions are alleles.
Answer: Alleles.
Common mistake: A genome is all the genes. A chromatid is half a chromosome. A codon is three bases.
Similar example: T and t are alleles of which gene? The height gene.

questions.text: Crossing an F1 individual with a homozygous recessive parent is called a
questions.explanation:
Concept: A test cross shows whether the F1 is homozygous dominant or heterozygous from the offspring ratio.
Step 1: An unknown genotype can be tested.
Step 2: Cross the individual with a homozygous recessive.
Step 3: This is a test cross.
Answer: Test cross.
Common mistake: A monohybrid cross follows one trait. A reciprocal cross swaps the sexes.
Similar example: In a test cross all offspring show the dominant trait. What is the genotype of the parent? Homozygous dominant.

questions.text: The sex chromosomes of a normal human male are
questions.explanation:
Concept: Females are XX. The father's sperm decides the sex of the child because it carries either X or Y.
Step 1: A woman has two X chromosomes.
Step 2: A man has one X and one Y.
Step 3: So the male is XY.
Answer: XY.
Common mistake: XX is a female. XXY is a disorder and YY does not occur normally.
Similar example: Which parent decides the sex of the child? The father.

questions.text: Colour blindness is inherited through
options: A recessive gene on the X chromosome
A dominant gene on the Y chromosome
questions.explanation:
Concept: It is sex-linked, so it shows up more often in males, who have only one X chromosome.
Step 1: Colour blindness is more common in men.
Step 2: The gene is on the X chromosome and is recessive.
Step 3: A man has only one X, so he needs just one copy to be colour blind.
Answer: A recessive gene on the X chromosome.
Common mistake: A Y-linked or autosomal dominant gene would not give this pattern.
Similar example: Can a carrier mother have a colour-blind son? Yes.

questions.text: The appendix in humans is an example of a
questions.explanation:
Concept: A vestigial organ has lost most or all of its original function. It is evidence that organisms have changed over time.
Step 1: The human appendix has no important function now.
Step 2: In plant eaters, such as the rabbit, it is large and digests cellulose.
Step 3: Such a reduced organ is a vestigial structure.
Answer: Vestigial structure.
Common mistake: Homologous structures have a similar plan but different jobs. Analogous structures have the same job but different plans.
Similar example: Name another vestigial organ. The tail bone (coccyx).

questions.text: The correct order of classification from the highest rank to the lowest is
options: Phylum, Kingdom, Class, Family, Order, Genus, Species
Kingdom, Class, Phylum, Order, Genus, Family, Species
Species, Genus, Family, Order, Class, Phylum, Kingdom
Kingdom, Phylum, Class, Order, Family, Genus, Species
questions.explanation:
Concept: Each rank includes the ones below it. A species is the smallest group and a kingdom is the largest.
Step 1: Start from the biggest group: the kingdom.
Step 2: Each kingdom is divided into phyla, then classes, orders, families, genera and species.
Step 3: So the order from highest to lowest is Kingdom, Phylum, Class, Order, Family, Genus, Species.
Answer: Kingdom, Phylum, Class, Order, Family, Genus, Species.
Common mistake: The other options swap Class and Phylum, or Genus and Family, or run the order backwards.
Similar example: Which is the smallest rank? Species.
Tip: King Philip Came Over For Good Soup.

questions.text: Bacteria are placed in the kingdom Monera because they
questions.explanation:
Concept: Bacteria are prokaryotes. Their DNA lies free in the cytoplasm and is not enclosed in a nuclear membrane.
Step 1: Look at the cell structure of a bacterium.
Step 2: Its DNA lies free in the cytoplasm with no nuclear membrane.
Step 3: Cells like this are prokaryotic, and they are put in Monera.
Answer: Have no true nucleus.
Common mistake: Most bacteria have no chlorophyll, their wall is not cellulose, and they are unicellular, not multicellular.
Similar example: Is yeast a prokaryote? No, it has a nucleus.

questions.text: Which of the following is a feature of bryophytes?
options: They have true leaves and stems with vascular tissue
They have rhizoids instead of true roots
questions.explanation:
Concept: Mosses and liverworts have no vascular tissue. Rhizoids anchor them and absorb water.
Step 1: Bryophytes are mosses and liverworts.
Step 2: They have no vascular tissue and no true roots.
Step 3: Instead they use hair-like rhizoids to anchor and absorb water.
Answer: They have rhizoids instead of true roots.
Common mistake: Xylem and phloem are in ferns and seed plants. Bryophytes make spores, not seeds.
Similar example: Which group has true roots but no seeds? Ferns.

questions.text: Which of the following animals has four pairs of walking legs?
questions.explanation:
Concept: Arachnids (spiders, scorpions, ticks) have four pairs of legs and no antennae. Insects have three pairs.
Step 1: Count the legs: four pairs means eight legs.
Step 2: Insects have three pairs, so housefly, butterfly and termite are out.
Step 3: The spider is an arachnid with four pairs.
Answer: Spider.
Common mistake: Housefly, butterfly and termite are insects with six legs.
Similar example: How many pairs of legs does a scorpion have? Four.

questions.text: The lateral line of a fish is used for
options: Detecting vibrations and pressure changes in the water
questions.explanation:
Concept: It is a row of sense organs along the sides of the body that picks up water movements.
Step 1: The lateral line is a row of pores along each side.
Step 2: It contains sensory cells in a canal.
Step 3: These detect vibrations and pressure changes in the water.
Answer: Detecting vibrations and pressure changes in the water.
Common mistake: Gaseous exchange is by gills, swimming is by fins and reproduction is by the gonads.
Similar example: Which organ do fish use for breathing? Gills.

questions.text: The cell organelle that packages and secretes substances such as enzymes is the
questions.explanation:
Concept: The Golgi apparatus modifies proteins and packs them into vesicles for secretion.
Step 1: Proteins made at the ribosomes must be processed.
Step 2: The stack of flattened sacs sorts, modifies and packs them into vesicles.
Step 3: That is the Golgi apparatus.
Answer: Golgi apparatus.
Common mistake: The nucleolus makes ribosomes, a centriole forms the spindle and a lysosome digests.
Similar example: Which organelle makes ribosomes? The nucleolus.

questions.text: The light reaction of photosynthesis takes place in the
questions.explanation:
Concept: Chlorophyll in the grana traps light energy, which splits water and makes ATP. The stroma is where carbon dioxide is fixed.
Step 1: Light energy must be trapped by chlorophyll.
Step 2: Chlorophyll is arranged in stacks called grana.
Step 3: So the light reaction occurs in the grana, and the dark stage in the stroma.
Answer: Grana of the chloroplast.
Common mistake: The stroma is where carbon dioxide is fixed. The mitochondrion is for respiration.
Similar example: Where does the dark reaction take place? In the stroma.

questions.text: Meiosis results in the formation of
questions.explanation:
Concept: One diploid cell divides twice, giving four daughter cells with half the chromosome number. These become the gametes.
Step 1: Meiosis has two divisions after one DNA replication.
Step 2: A diploid cell makes four cells.
Step 3: Each has half the chromosome number, so they are haploid.
Answer: Four haploid cells.
Common mistake: Mitosis makes two diploid cells. Four diploid cells or two haploid cells are wrong counts.
Similar example: How many cells does mitosis make from one? Two.

questions.text: Which reagent is used to test for starch?
questions.explanation:
Concept: Iodine solution turns blue-black with starch. Benedict's is for reducing sugar and biuret is for protein.
Step 1: Each food class has its own test.
Step 2: Starch gives a blue-black colour with a brown solution.
Step 3: That solution is iodine.
Answer: Iodine solution.
Common mistake: Benedict's tests reducing sugar, biuret tests protein and Millon's tests protein too.
Similar example: Which reagent tests for reducing sugar? Benedict's solution.

questions.text: Bile helps digestion by
questions.explanation:
Concept: Bile salts break large fat globules into tiny droplets, which gives lipase a larger surface to work on.
Step 1: Bile is made in the liver and stored in the gall bladder.
Step 2: It contains no enzymes.
Step 3: Bile salts break big fat globules into tiny droplets, which is emulsification.
Answer: Emulsifying fats.
Common mistake: Proteins and starch are digested by enzymes. Killing bacteria is done by stomach acid.
Similar example: Which enzyme digests fat? Lipase.

questions.text: Which of the following is a carnivorous plant?
questions.explanation:
Concept: Pitcher plants trap and digest insects to get nitrogen compounds. Mistletoe and Cuscuta are parasites and a mushroom is a fungus.
Step 1: Carnivorous plants catch and digest insects.
Step 2: Mistletoe and Cuscuta are parasites on other plants.
Step 3: The pitcher plant traps insects in a jug-shaped leaf.
Answer: Pitcher plant.
Common mistake: Mistletoe and Cuscuta are parasites. A mushroom is a fungus.
Similar example: Name another insect-eating plant. Venus fly trap.

questions.text: The blood group known as the universal donor is
questions.explanation:
Concept: Group O red cells have no A or B antigens, so they are not attacked by the recipient's antibodies.
Step 1: Look at the antigens on the red cells.
Step 2: Group O has none, so the recipient's antibodies find nothing to attack.
Step 3: So group O can be given to all groups.
Answer: O.
Common mistake: Groups A, B and AB have antigens that may be attacked.
Similar example: Which group is the universal recipient? AB.

questions.text: Blood vessels that carry blood away from the heart are
questions.explanation:
Concept: Arteries have thick, elastic, muscular walls to withstand the high pressure of blood leaving the heart.
Step 1: Name the three vessel types: arteries, veins, capillaries.
Step 2: Arteries carry blood away from the heart at high pressure.
Step 3: Veins carry it back.
Answer: Arteries.
Common mistake: Veins return blood to the heart. Capillaries link arteries and veins. Venules are small veins.
Similar example: Which vessels carry blood to the heart? Veins.
Tip: Arteries = Away.

questions.text: Manufactured food in plants is transported through the
questions.explanation:
Concept: Sieve tubes in the phloem carry sugars from the leaves to the storage and growing regions. This is translocation.
Step 1: Food is made in the leaves.
Step 2: It must travel to roots, fruits and growing points.
Step 3: The sieve tubes of the phloem carry it.
Answer: Phloem.
Common mistake: Xylem carries water. The cambium makes new cells. The cortex stores.
Similar example: What carries water up? Xylem.

questions.text: All of the following are features of a good respiratory surface EXCEPT that it is
questions.explanation:
Concept: A good gaseous exchange surface is thin, moist and has a rich blood supply and a large surface area.
Step 1: List the features: thin, moist, large area, rich blood supply.
Step 2: Check each option against the list.
Step 3: 'Thick and dry' does not belong, because gases dissolve in moisture and a thick wall slows diffusion.
Answer: Thick and dry.
Common mistake: The other three are features of a good gaseous exchange surface.
Similar example: Is a moist surface needed? Yes, gases dissolve in it.

questions.text: The first stage of respiration, glycolysis, takes place in the
questions.explanation:
Concept: Glycolysis breaks glucose into two pyruvate molecules in the cytoplasm and needs no oxygen.
Step 1: Glycolysis means breaking down glucose.
Step 2: It needs no oxygen.
Step 3: It takes place in the cytoplasm and gives pyruvate.
Answer: Cytoplasm.
Common mistake: The mitochondrion carries out the later stages. The nucleus and chloroplast are not involved.
Similar example: Where does the Krebs cycle take place? In the mitochondrion.

questions.text: The excretory organs of insects are the
questions.explanation:
Concept: Malpighian tubules take waste from the haemolymph and pass it into the gut as uric acid.
Step 1: Insects have an open circulatory system.
Step 2: Long thin tubes take wastes from the blood.
Step 3: They are the Malpighian tubules.
Answer: Malpighian tubules.
Common mistake: Nephridia are in earthworms, flame cells in flatworms and kidneys in vertebrates.
Similar example: What do earthworms use for excretion? Nephridia.

questions.text: The antidiuretic hormone (ADH) regulates the
options: Reabsorption of water in the kidney
questions.explanation:
Concept: ADH makes the collecting duct more permeable to water, so less water is lost in the urine.
Step 1: ADH is made when the blood is too concentrated.
Step 2: It makes the collecting duct more permeable to water.
Step 3: So more water is reabsorbed and urine is small and concentrated.
Answer: Reabsorption of water in the kidney.
Common mistake: ADH does not control glucose, urea formation or filtration.
Similar example: What happens to urine when we drink much water? It becomes dilute.

questions.text: The exoskeleton of insects is made of
questions.explanation:
Concept: Chitin forms the hard outer covering that protects insects and stops water loss.
Step 1: The exoskeleton is a hard covering on the outside.
Step 2: It prevents water loss and protects the body.
Step 3: It is made of chitin.
Answer: Chitin.
Common mistake: Cellulose is in plant walls. Keratin is in hair and nails. Cartilage is an internal skeleton.
Similar example: What are fungal cell walls made of? Chitin.

questions.text: Which of the following has a hydrostatic skeleton?
questions.explanation:
Concept: The earthworm moves by contracting its circular and longitudinal muscles against the fluid in its body cavity.
Step 1: A hydrostatic skeleton is fluid held under pressure.
Step 2: Soft-bodied animals have it.
Step 3: The earthworm uses it with its circular and longitudinal muscles.
Answer: Earthworm.
Common mistake: Cockroach has an exoskeleton. Frog and lizard have an internal bony skeleton.
Similar example: Which animal moves by squeezing its body fluid? Earthworm.

questions.text: Double fertilisation is a characteristic of
questions.explanation:
Concept: In angiosperms one sperm nucleus fuses with the egg to form a zygote and the other fuses with the polar nuclei to form the endosperm.
Step 1: Two fertilisations happen inside the embryo sac.
Step 2: One sperm nucleus fuses with the egg to give a zygote.
Step 3: The other fuses with the polar nuclei to give endosperm. This occurs only in flowering plants.
Answer: Flowering plants.
Common mistake: Ferns, mosses and conifers have only a single fertilisation.
Similar example: What does the zygote become? The embryo.

questions.text: The menstrual cycle in a woman is on average about
questions.explanation:
Concept: Menstruation lasts about 5 days, and ovulation takes place near day 14.
Step 1: Count from the first day of bleeding.
Step 2: Menstruation lasts about 5 days and ovulation occurs about day 14.
Step 3: The cycle ends after about 28 days.
Answer: 28 days.
Common mistake: 14, 21 and 40 days are not the usual cycle length.
Similar example: On which day does ovulation occur? About day 14.

questions.text: In the male reproductive system, sperm are produced in the
questions.explanation:
Concept: Sperm are made in the testes and stored in the epididymis.
Step 1: Sperm are made in the testes.
Step 2: Inside the testes, coiled tubes make them.
Step 3: They are the seminiferous tubules.
Answer: Seminiferous tubules of the testes.
Common mistake: The epididymis stores sperm. The vas deferens carries it. The prostate makes fluid.
Similar example: Where are sperm stored? Epididymis.

questions.text: Which of the following is a feature of wind-pollinated flowers?
questions.explanation:
Concept: Wind-pollinated flowers have light, abundant pollen and large feathery stigmas, and are small and dull.
Step 1: Wind carries pollen at random, so much pollen is needed.
Step 2: Pollen must be light and the stigma must catch it.
Step 3: Feathery stigmas do this.
Answer: Feathery stigmas.
Common mistake: Bright petals and nectar attract insects, and sticky pollen is for insect pollination.
Similar example: Is grass pollinated by wind or insects? Wind.

questions.text: The stage in the life cycle of a housefly in which the larva changes into an adult is the
questions.explanation:
Concept: The housefly has complete metamorphosis: egg, larva (maggot), pupa, adult.
Step 1: Complete metamorphosis has four stages.
Step 2: They are egg, larva (maggot), pupa and adult.
Step 3: The change from larva to adult occurs in the pupa.
Answer: Pupa.
Common mistake: The egg comes first. Nymph is for incomplete metamorphosis. Imago is the adult.
Similar example: How many stages has a cockroach? Three, with a nymph.

questions.text: The part of the ear that helps in maintaining balance is the
questions.explanation:
Concept: The semicircular canals contain fluid and sensory hairs that detect head rotation.
Step 1: The ear has three parts: outer, middle and inner.
Step 2: The inner ear has the cochlea (for hearing) and the semicircular canals.
Step 3: The semicircular canals detect head movement.
Answer: Semicircular canals.
Common mistake: The cochlea is for hearing. The ear drum and ossicles carry sound.
Similar example: Which part of the ear detects sound? The cochlea.

questions.text: Deficiency of iodine in the diet can cause
questions.explanation:
Concept: The thyroid gland needs iodine to make thyroxine. Without it the gland enlarges, giving goitre.
Step 1: The thyroid gland makes thyroxine.
Step 2: Thyroxine needs iodine.
Step 3: Without iodine the gland swells, giving goitre.
Answer: Goitre.
Common mistake: Scurvy is lack of vitamin C, rickets is lack of vitamin D and anaemia is lack of iron.
Similar example: Which mineral is lacking in anaemia? Iron.

questions.text: The part of the brain that regulates body temperature is the
questions.explanation:
Concept: The hypothalamus is the temperature thermostat of the body. It triggers sweating, shivering and changes in blood flow.
Step 1: Body temperature must be about 37 degrees Celsius.
Step 2: A part under the cerebrum monitors the blood temperature.
Step 3: It is the hypothalamus.
Answer: Hypothalamus.
Common mistake: The cerebellum controls balance. The medulla controls breathing. The cerebrum is for thought.
Similar example: Which gland does the hypothalamus control? The pituitary gland.

questions.text: An orchid growing on the trunk of a tree is an example of
questions.explanation:
Concept: The orchid gets support and light and the tree is neither helped nor harmed.
Step 1: The orchid sits on the tree for support and light.
Step 2: It does not take food from the tree.
Step 3: The orchid gains and the tree is unaffected, so it is commensalism.
Answer: Commensalism.
Common mistake: A parasite harms the host. Mutualism helps both. Predation kills.
Similar example: Barnacles on a whale are an example of? Commensalism.

questions.text: The role of decomposers in an ecosystem is to
options: Break down dead organic matter and return nutrients to the soil
questions.explanation:
Concept: Bacteria and fungi decay dead organisms, releasing minerals that plants can reuse.
Step 1: Dead plants and animals contain nutrients.
Step 2: Bacteria and fungi digest them.
Step 3: The nutrients go back to the soil for plants to use.
Answer: Break down dead organic matter and return nutrients to the soil.
Common mistake: Trapping solar energy and producing oxygen is for plants. Feeding on living plants is for herbivores.
Similar example: Name a decomposer. A mushroom or bacteria.

questions.text: Which instrument is used to estimate the population of grass in a field?
questions.explanation:
Concept: A quadrat is a square frame placed at random in the field. The plants inside are counted and the numbers scaled up.
Step 1: Counting every blade of grass is not practical.
Step 2: A square frame is thrown at random and the plants inside it are counted.
Step 3: That frame is a quadrat.
Answer: Quadrat.
Common mistake: A pitfall trap catches ground insects. A sweep net catches flying insects. A hygrometer measures humidity.
Similar example: What does a pitfall trap catch? Crawling insects.

questions.text: Which gas released from burning fossil fuels is mainly responsible for acid rain?
questions.explanation:
Concept: Sulphur dioxide and oxides of nitrogen dissolve in rain water and form acids.
Step 1: Fossil fuels contain sulphur.
Step 2: Burning them releases a gas that dissolves in rain water.
Step 3: That gas is sulphur dioxide, which forms acid rain.
Answer: Sulphur dioxide.
Common mistake: Carbon monoxide is poisonous but is not the main acid rain gas. Oxygen and hydrogen do not cause acid rain.
Similar example: What is the pH of acid rain? Below 5.6.

questions.text: The soil water that is most useful to plants is
questions.explanation:
Concept: Capillary water is held as a film around soil particles and plant roots can absorb it. Gravitational water drains away.
Step 1: Soil holds water in several forms.
Step 2: Gravitational water drains away, and hygroscopic water is held too tightly.
Step 3: Capillary water is held in the small pores, so roots can take it.
Answer: Capillary water.
Common mistake: Hygroscopic water is too tightly held and gravitational water drains away.
Similar example: Which water drains down after rain? Gravitational water.

questions.text: An adaptation that reduces water loss in desert plants is
options: Many stomata on the upper surface
questions.explanation:
Concept: Small leaves or spines have a small surface area, so little water is lost by transpiration.
Step 1: Water is lost through the leaf surface.
Step 2: A small surface area loses less water.
Step 3: Reduced leaves or spines do this.
Answer: Reduced leaves or spines.
Common mistake: Large thin leaves, many stomata and shallow roots would lose more water.
Similar example: Why do cacti store water? Their stems are fleshy.

questions.text: Which of the following is a method of wildlife conservation?
options: Setting up game reserves and national parks
questions.explanation:
Concept: Protected areas keep animals and their habitats safe from hunting and destruction.
Step 1: Conservation protects animals and their habitats.
Step 2: Burning, clearing and hunting destroy them.
Step 3: Setting aside game reserves and national parks protects them.
Answer: Setting up game reserves and national parks.
Common mistake: Bush burning, forest clearing and hunting in the breeding season reduce wildlife.
Similar example: Name a national park in Nigeria. Kainji Lake National Park.

questions.text: An organism with two different alleles for a trait is said to be
questions.explanation:
Concept: Tt is heterozygous. TT and tt are homozygous.
Step 1: Write the alleles: a heterozygote has two different ones, such as Tt.
Step 2: Two same alleles make a homozygote.
Step 3: So the organism is heterozygous.
Answer: Heterozygous.
Common mistake: TT is homozygous dominant and tt is homozygous recessive. Hemizygous is used for genes on the X in males.
Similar example: Is Aa heterozygous? Yes.

questions.text: Which of the following can cause mutation?
questions.explanation:
Concept: Radiation such as X-rays, gamma rays and ultraviolet light, and some chemicals, can damage DNA.
Step 1: A mutation is a change in DNA.
Step 2: High-energy radiation damages the DNA.
Step 3: X-rays do this.
Answer: X-rays.
Common mistake: Visible light, water and carbon dioxide do not damage DNA.
Similar example: Name another mutagen. Ultraviolet light.

questions.text: A cross between red-flowered and white-flowered snapdragons gives pink-flowered offspring. This is an example of
questions.explanation:
Concept: Neither allele is completely dominant, so the heterozygote has an intermediate colour.
Step 1: Red x white gives pink.
Step 2: Neither allele hides the other.
Step 3: This is incomplete dominance.
Answer: Incomplete dominance.
Common mistake: In complete dominance one allele hides the other, so the offspring would be red.
Similar example: Pink x pink gives what ratio? 1 red : 2 pink : 1 white.

questions.text: If both parents are carriers (AS) of the sickle-cell gene, the probability that a child is SS is
questions.explanation:
Concept: AS x AS gives 1 AA : 2 AS : 1 SS. One in four (25%) is SS.
Step 1: Write the cross: AS x AS.
Step 2: Gametes: A and S from each. Combine: AA, AS, AS, SS.
Step 3: One of four is SS, which is 25%.
Answer: 25%.
Common mistake: 50% would be for AS and 75% is for the offspring not SS.
Similar example: What is the chance of an AS child? 50%.

questions.text: The spread of dark-coloured peppered moths in industrial areas is evidence of
questions.explanation:
Concept: Soot-darkened tree trunks made light moths easy for birds to see. Dark moths survived and passed on their genes.
Step 1: Soot made tree trunks dark.
Step 2: Pale moths were easily seen and eaten by birds.
Step 3: Dark moths survived and bred, which is natural selection.
Answer: Natural selection.
Common mistake: Use and disuse is Lamarck's idea. Artificial selection needs humans.
Similar example: What is the name of this change in colour? Industrial melanism.

questions.text: Fungi differ from green plants in that fungi
questions.explanation:
Concept: Fungi are heterotrophs. They feed on dead or living organic matter and store food as glycogen.
Step 1: Compare how each group gets food.
Step 2: Green plants have chlorophyll and make food by photosynthesis.
Step 3: Fungi have no chlorophyll and absorb food from other organisms.
Answer: Lack chlorophyll.
Common mistake: Fungi have no chloroplasts and cannot make their own food.
Similar example: How do fungi digest food? They release enzymes outside their bodies.

questions.text: Which feature distinguishes reptiles from amphibians?
questions.explanation:
Concept: Reptiles have a dry, waterproof skin with scales and lay shelled eggs on land. Amphibians have moist skin.
Step 1: Both groups are vertebrates with four limbs and lungs.
Step 2: Amphibians have a moist skin with no scales.
Step 3: Reptiles have a dry skin covered with scales.
Answer: Dry scaly skin.
Common mistake: Lungs, a backbone and four limbs are shared by both groups.
Similar example: Which group lays eggs with shells on land? Reptiles.

questions.text: Which of the following is an adaptation of birds for flight?
questions.explanation:
Concept: Air spaces in the bones reduce the body weight. Birds also have feathers and strong flight muscles.
Step 1: Flight needs a light body.
Step 2: Birds have hollow bones filled with air spaces.
Step 3: They also have feathers and strong breast muscles.
Answer: Light, hollow bones.
Common mistake: Scaly legs, a toothless bill and webbed feet are not for flying.
Similar example: Why do birds lack teeth? Teeth are heavy.

questions.text: Which of the following is a gymnosperm?
questions.explanation:
Concept: Gymnosperms bear naked seeds in cones. Pines and cycads are examples.
Step 1: Gymnosperms have naked seeds on cones.
Step 2: Maize, mango and cowpea bear seeds in fruits.
Step 3: The pine bears cones, so it is a gymnosperm.
Answer: Pine.
Common mistake: Maize, mango and cowpea are flowering plants (angiosperms).
Similar example: Name another gymnosperm. Cycad.

questions.text: A dichotomous key is used for
questions.explanation:
Concept: At each step you choose between two statements until you reach the name of the organism.
Step 1: Dichotomous means 'divided into two'.
Step 2: At each step you choose between two statements.
Step 3: Following the choices leads you to the name of the organism.
Answer: Identifying organisms.
Common mistake: It is not used for counting, measuring growth or testing food.
Similar example: What do you need to use a key? The specimen to observe.

questions.text: A red blood cell placed in distilled water will
questions.explanation:
Concept: Water enters the cell by osmosis. The cell has no wall and so it bursts (haemolysis).
Step 1: Distilled water has a higher water potential than the cell.
Step 2: Water enters the cell by osmosis.
Step 3: An animal cell has no cell wall, so it swells and bursts.
Answer: Swell and burst.
Common mistake: A cell shrinks in a strong salt solution, not in pure water.
Similar example: What happens to a red cell in strong salt solution? It shrinks.

questions.text: The shrinking of the protoplasm of a plant cell away from the cell wall in a strong salt solution is
questions.explanation:
Concept: Water leaves the cell by osmosis. The cell becomes flaccid and then plasmolysed.
Step 1: The solution outside is stronger than the cell sap.
Step 2: Water leaves the cell by osmosis.
Step 3: The protoplasm pulls away from the wall. This is plasmolysis.
Answer: Plasmolysis.
Common mistake: Haemolysis is bursting of red cells. Turgidity is a swollen cell. Imbibition is absorption by dry seeds.
Similar example: What is a swollen plant cell called? Turgid.

questions.text: The nucleolus is the site of
questions.explanation:
Concept: The nucleolus makes ribosomal RNA, which is used to build ribosomes.
Step 1: The nucleolus is a dark body in the nucleus.
Step 2: It makes ribosomal RNA.
Step 3: The rRNA joins protein to make ribosomes.
Answer: Ribosomal RNA synthesis.
Common mistake: Photosynthesis is in chloroplasts, ATP in mitochondria and protein digestion in lysosomes.
Similar example: Where is DNA kept? In the nucleus.

questions.text: A deficiency of vitamin D in children causes
questions.explanation:
Concept: Vitamin D helps the body absorb calcium. Without it the bones are soft and the legs become bowed.
Step 1: Vitamin D helps the gut absorb calcium.
Step 2: Without calcium the bones are soft.
Step 3: In children the legs bend, and the disease is rickets.
Answer: Rickets.
Common mistake: Scurvy is vitamin C, beriberi is vitamin B1 and pellagra is niacin.
Similar example: Which mineral is needed for strong bones? Calcium.

questions.text: Most absorption of digested food takes place in the
questions.explanation:
Concept: The ileum is long and has villi with a rich blood supply, which gives a large surface for absorption.
Step 1: Digestion is completed in the small intestine.
Step 2: The last part of it, the ileum, is long and folded.
Step 3: Its villi give a large surface and have a rich blood supply.
Answer: Ileum.
Common mistake: The stomach absorbs little. The oesophagus only carries food. The colon absorbs water.
Similar example: What does the colon absorb? Water.

questions.text: The wave-like contraction of muscles that moves food along the alimentary canal is
questions.explanation:
Concept: The circular and longitudinal muscles contract and relax in turn behind the food and push it forward.
Step 1: Food does not fall by gravity alone.
Step 2: Muscle rings contract behind the food and relax in front.
Step 3: This pushes food along, and is called peristalsis.
Answer: Peristalsis.
Common mistake: Emulsification is breaking fat. Mastication is chewing. Egestion is removing faeces.
Similar example: What is chewing called? Mastication.

questions.text: The mammalian circulatory system is described as double because blood
options: Flows in two directions in the veins
Passes through the heart twice in one complete circuit
questions.explanation:
Concept: Blood goes through the right side to the lungs and returns to the left side before it is sent to the body.
Step 1: Follow one drop of blood around.
Step 2: From the right side of the heart it goes to the lungs and back to the left side.
Step 3: Then it goes to the body and back to the right side, passing through the heart twice.
Answer: Passes through the heart twice in one complete circuit.
Common mistake: It is one heart with two pumps and not two hearts.
Similar example: Is a fish circulation single or double? Single.

questions.text: Lymph differs from blood in that lymph has no
questions.explanation:
Concept: Lymph is tissue fluid that has entered lymph vessels. It contains lymphocytes but no red blood cells.
Step 1: Lymph is tissue fluid collected by lymph vessels.
Step 2: It carries lymphocytes and fats.
Step 3: It does not have red blood cells.
Answer: Red blood cells.
Common mistake: Lymph has white cells, water and dissolved food.
Similar example: Which vessels collect tissue fluid? Lymph vessels.

questions.text: The ascent of water in tall trees is best explained by the
questions.explanation:
Concept: Water evaporates from the leaves and pulls up an unbroken column of water in the xylem, because water molecules stick to each other (cohesion).
Step 1: Water evaporates from the leaf cells.
Step 2: This pulls water up the xylem in an unbroken column because water molecules cling together (cohesion).
Step 3: This is the cohesion-tension theory.
Answer: Cohesion-tension theory.
Common mistake: The pressure flow theory explains food movement in the phloem.
Similar example: Which tissue moves water in a tree? Xylem.

questions.text: Gaseous exchange in insects takes place through
questions.explanation:
Concept: Air enters the spiracles and goes through branching tracheae to the tissues.
Step 1: Insects have no lungs or gills.
Step 2: Air enters through small holes called spiracles.
Step 3: Branched tubes (tracheae) carry it to the cells.
Answer: Tracheae and spiracles.
Common mistake: Gills are for fish and book lungs are for spiders.
Similar example: What are the openings of an insect called? Spiracles.

questions.text: The energy currency of the cell is
questions.explanation:
Concept: Respiration uses the energy in glucose to make ATP, which cells then use for work.
Step 1: Cells need energy for work.
Step 2: The energy from glucose is stored in a small molecule.
Step 3: That molecule is ATP.
Answer: ATP.
Common mistake: DNA stores genetic information. Glucose is a fuel. Haemoglobin carries oxygen.
Similar example: How many ATP does aerobic respiration yield? About 38 per glucose.

questions.text: Sweat contains mainly
options: Water, salts and a little urea
questions.explanation:
Concept: Sweat cools the body as it evaporates and also removes small amounts of waste.
Step 1: Sweat is made by the sweat glands in the skin.
Step 2: It is mostly water with salts.
Step 3: It also has a small amount of urea.
Answer: Water, salts and a little urea.
Common mistake: Glucose and proteins are not found in sweat. Bile salts come from the liver.
Similar example: What is the main function of sweating? Cooling the body.

questions.text: The release of water droplets from the leaf margins of plants such as grass at night occurs through the
questions.explanation:
Concept: This is called guttation. It occurs when root pressure is high and the air is humid.
Step 1: Water droplets form on grass tips at night.
Step 2: They come from special pores at the leaf edge.
Step 3: These are the hydathodes, and the process is guttation.
Answer: Hydathodes.
Common mistake: Stomata lose water vapour. Lenticels are for gaseous exchange in stems.
Similar example: Does guttation lose liquid water or vapour? Liquid water.

questions.text: The long bone of the thigh is the
questions.explanation:
Concept: The femur is the longest and strongest bone in the body. The humerus is in the upper arm.
Step 1: The thigh is in the upper leg.
Step 2: The upper leg bone is the femur.
Step 3: It is the longest and strongest bone.
Answer: Femur.
Common mistake: The humerus is in the upper arm. The tibia is the shin bone. The radius is in the forearm.
Similar example: Which bone is the upper arm bone? Humerus.

questions.text: The bones of the skull are joined by
questions.explanation:
Concept: The sutures between skull bones do not allow movement, so the brain is well protected.
Step 1: The skull protects the brain.
Step 2: It must not move.
Step 3: Its bones are joined by fixed joints called sutures.
Answer: Fixed (immovable) joints.
Common mistake: Ball-and-socket, hinge and pivot joints all allow movement.
Similar example: Which joint allows movement at the elbow? Hinge joint.

questions.text: The part of the flower that produces pollen grains is the
questions.explanation:
Concept: Pollen is made in the pollen sacs of the anther, which is part of the stamen.
Step 1: The male part of a flower is the stamen.
Step 2: The stamen has a filament and an anther.
Step 3: The anther makes the pollen.
Answer: Anther.
Common mistake: The stigma receives pollen. The ovary holds ovules. The style joins the stigma and ovary.
Similar example: Which part receives pollen? The stigma.

questions.text: A fruit that develops without fertilisation is described as
questions.explanation:
Concept: Seedless bananas and some oranges develop this way.
Step 1: Usually a fruit forms after fertilisation.
Step 2: Some plants form fruits without it.
Step 3: These fruits have no seeds and are parthenocarpic.
Answer: Parthenocarpic.
Common mistake: Aggregate, dehiscent and succulent describe other fruit types.
Similar example: Name a seedless fruit. Banana.

questions.text: The hormone that maintains pregnancy is
questions.explanation:
Concept: Progesterone keeps the uterine lining thick and prevents menstruation.
Step 1: The uterus lining must stay thick.
Step 2: The corpus luteum and later the placenta make a hormone to keep it.
Step 3: That hormone is progesterone.
Answer: Progesterone.
Common mistake: FSH and LH act before ovulation. Adrenaline is for emergencies.
Similar example: Which hormone starts the growth of a follicle? FSH.

questions.text: Amoeba reproduces by
questions.explanation:
Concept: The nucleus divides by mitosis and then the cytoplasm divides into two equal daughter cells.
Step 1: Amoeba is a single cell.
Step 2: Its nucleus divides, then the cytoplasm divides.
